title: HeritageRAG study report
text:
What is this study about?
Historians and other researchers now find most of their sources through computer systems. Between a research question and the evidence on the screen there are several hidden steps: catalogues from many institutions, lists of official subject words, automatic indexing tools and, more and more, AI that writes summaries.
These steps help, but they also make choices for us. They decide which words count, which records come first and which collections appear at all. This study makes those steps visible and measures what each step changes.
crumbs: 1  How the way we search changes what we find

title: HeritageRAG study report
text:
The three ways of searching
Think of asking a library for material on how women were shown in Finnish advertising, 1920 to 1960. We picked two key words, women and advertising, and searched in three ways:
Search A: your own words using Finna We search for exactly the words we chose.

women AND advertising

Search B: your words + the indexer’s suggestions A computer tool called Annif reads the question and suggests subject words, the way a cataloguer would. We add the suggestions that fit one of our words.

(women OR “view of women”) AND advertising

Search C: B + official thesaurus terms The national thesaurus YSO (looked up through the Finto service) gives the official name of each idea in Finnish, Swedish and English. We add those as well.

(women OR “view of women” OR naiset OR kvinnor OR naiskuva OR kvinnobilden) AND (advertising OR mainonta OR reklam)

AND means “both must appear” and OR means “any of these will do”. So every search keeps the whole topic (women and advertising); the searches differ only in how many ways of saying each idea they accept.

title: HeritageRAG study report
text:
What we did

We wrote 13 research questions on different topics and periods, each with two key words.
We searched Finna in the three ways above, with the same year range for all three.
From each search we kept the top 60 records, in Finna’s own order.
We recorded why each record was found: which word matched it.
An AI model (OpenAI) read the top 8 records of each search and wrote a short answer, citing the records it used.
We compared the three searches, and the three answers, with each other.

2. Annif suggests subject words
Annif is a tool made by the National Library of Finland. It reads a text and suggests subject words from the official thesaurus, as a cataloguer would. It gives each suggestion a confidence score between 0 and 1.
We reach Annif through our R package annif (version 0.1.1), which sends the question to the public Finto AI service and only reads its answer. Annif’s models are retrained from time to time, so the run records which model answered: yso-en (backend nn_ensemble, model last changed 2025-09-16); yso-fi (backend nn_ensemble, model last changed 2025-09-16).
We keep a suggestion only if it fits one of our key words. It fits when it is the same idea, a closely related idea in the thesaurus, or shares the start of a word with it (advertising and advertisements). A suggestion that is only a piece of a key word phrase (Finland for Finland Swedes) is not added, because it would make the search wider than the idea. Suggestions that fit none of our words are written down but not searched. They show how the computer would have framed the question differently.

The top 8 records of each search go to an AI model (here from OpenAI), with strict rules: use only these records, say when the evidence is too thin, and put the record numbers after every sentence that says something about the records. So each search gets its own answer.

title: 3  How the study works, step by step
text:
Words used in this report


Finna

The national search service for Finnish libraries, archives and museums. All records in this study come from it.

Annif

An automatic subject-indexing tool from the National Library of Finland, offered as the public service Finto AI. It suggests subject words for a text. We use it through the R package annif.

YSO

The General Finnish Ontology: the official list of subject words, with names in Finnish, Swedish and English.

Finto

The online service where YSO and other Finnish vocabularies are published. We use it to look up YSO.

Key word (anchor)

One of the two to four core ideas the researcher picks for a question, e.g. women and advertising.

Search A, B, C

A uses only your key words. B adds Annif’s suggestions that fit them. C adds YSO’s official names in three languages.

Query

The exact text sent to Finna. AND means both ideas must appear; OR means any of the listed words will do.

Matching records (size of the search)

How many records in the whole Finna index match a search. It shows how wide the search is.

Records kept

The top 60 records of a search, in Finna’s order. All comparisons use these.

Evidence

The top 8 records that the AI reads before writing its answer.

Overlap

How many records two searches have in common. We use the Jaccard share: records found by both, divided by records found by either. 1 means the same records, 0 means none shared.

Rank overlap (RBO)

Like overlap, but it cares most about the top of the list. Two searches that agree on their first few records score high even if they differ further down.

Difference in mix (JSD)

The Jensen-Shannon divergence. A number from 0 to 1 that compares two mixes, for example of institutions. 0 = exactly the same mix; 1 = nothing in common. Around 0.1 is a small change; above 0.5 is a big one.

Uncertainty range

Because we only look at 60 records, a mix could look different just by chance. The range shows the values that are believable given the records we have.

Diversity

How many different institutions (or languages) a search shows, counting rare ones less. Ten equally common institutions give a diversity of 10.

Hidden match

A record that matches a search, but none of the search words appear in the parts of the record that Finna shows us.

Claim

One sentence of an AI answer.

Citation

A record number in square brackets after a sentence, for example [werstas.we-1372484].

Blinded checking

The checkers see the records and sentences mixed up, without knowing which search they came from, so their judgement is fair.

What it means. Most suggestions (59%) did not fit the researcher’s words. Annif suggested history for 12 of the 13 questions: it reads “how did X change” as a question about history in general. Other suggestions that did not fit show a different way of describing the topic: migration (demography) (Emigrant letters); towns and cities (Working-class housing); Karelians (Karelian evacuees); woman’s status (Women’s suffrage); historia (Women in advertising (asked in Finnish)); Finns (Emigrant letters); Finnish Americans (Emigrant letters); Finland (Karelian evacuees).
These words were not searched in this study. They are a finding in themselves: they show how an automatic indexer would redraw the question’s boundaries. For the Karelian evacuees question, Annif’s internally displaced persons is in fact the official term, while the everyday word evacuees found nothing. Likewise, for Swedish-language theatre Annif suggested Swedish-speaking Finns, the thesaurus’s name for the group, while the everyday Finland Swedes found nothing.

NoteWomen in advertising (asked in English)





Search A: your own words

Observations:

A 1921 advertising record is catalogued as a political advertisement linked to a women’s organisation titled “Me odotamme sinua” (Social Democratic Women’s Union). [werstas.we-1372484].
A 1950 poster record is catalogued with subjects that include women’s rights movements and the cooperative system. [ta_ah.ta-1369756].
A 1955 Asko advertising photograph record is catalogued with subjects that include women and newspaper advertising as well as domestic goods (coffee cups, curtains, carpets, sofas). [lahdenmuseo.lkm-461598].
Three 1956 product-ad records from OTK’s shirt factory are catalogued with subjects including women, shirts, mannequins (occupations), and advertising photographs. [werstas.we-1613705, werstas.we-1613706, werstas.we-1613707].
Two 1960 catalogue records from textile/wool manufacturers are catalogued with subjects that include women, advertising, marketing, and clothing items such as trousers and blankets; one of these records’ title references the year 1931 while its recorded year is 1960. [hyvinkaa_mui.mui-25099, hyvinkaa_mui.mui-25159].

Interpretation (separate from the direct observations above):

The metadata in the retrieved records suggests that advertising involving women appears in both explicitly political/organisational contexts (1921) and in consumer, home, and clothing contexts in the 1950s–1960s. [werstas.we-1372484; ta_ah.ta-1369756; lahdenmuseo.lkm-461598; werstas.we-1613705, werstas.we-1613706, werstas.we-1613707; hyvinkaa_mui.mui-25099, hyvinkaa_mui.mui-25159].
The 1950 record’s subjects indicate that references to women’s rights and cooperatives persisted into mid-century advertising metadata as well as the later consumer-oriented records. [ta_ah.ta-1369756; lahdenmuseo.lkm-461598; werstas.we-1613705, werstas.we-1613706, werstas.we-1613707; hyvinkaa_mui.mui-25099].

Limitations and caution:

The available evidence set is small and unevenly distributed across the four decades covered, so it is insufficient to support a general or definitive claim about broad changes in representations of women in Finnish advertising between 1920 and 1960. [werstas.we-1372484; ta_ah.ta-1369756; lahdenmuseo.lkm-461598; werstas.we-1613705, werstas.we-1613706, werstas.we-1613707; hyvinkaa_mui.mui-25099, hyvinkaa_mui.mui-25159].
I have relied only on the supplied catalogue metadata; I have not assumed or described the visual or textual content beyond those metadata fields. [werstas.we-1372484; ta_ah.ta-1369756; lahdenmuseo.lkm-461598; werstas.we-1613705, werstas.we-1613706, werstas.we-1613707; hyvinkaa_mui.mui-25099, hyvinkaa_mui.mui-25159].

Recommendation:

To assess change over time with confidence, consult a larger sample of primary advertising images and their full catalog or item records (visual content and full descriptions) from each decade.


Search B: your words + the indexer’s suggestions

Direct observations (based only on the provided catalogue metadata):

The 1921 record is titled “Mainos; ‘Me odotamme sinua’, Sosialidemokraattinen Työläisnaisliitto” and its subjects list advertisements, women’s organisations and political advertising [werstas.we-1372484].
A 1950 poster record is catalogued as “Juliste; KK:n juliste 1950:195” with subjects including women’s rights movements, the cooperative system and advertising [ta_ah.ta-1369756].
A record titled “Yhdistyneet Villatehtaat. Mainoskuva naisten arkiasusta vuodelta 1931.” is present with a year field of 1960 and subjects listing women, advertising and trousers [hyvinkaa_mui.mui-25159].
A 1960 record “Villayhtymä Oy. Mainoskuva matkahuovasta.” has subjects including wool industry, textile industry, women, marketing and advertising photographs [hyvinkaa_mui.mui-25099].
A 1955 record “Askon mainoskuva vuodelta 1955” lists subjects such as coffee cups, curtains, carpets and rugs, women, newspaper advertising, furniture and coffee culture [lahdenmuseo.lkm-461598].
Three 1956 records titled “OTK:n paitatehtaan tuotemainos” list subjects including advertisements, advertising photographs, mannequins (occupations), women and shirts, and give a Helsinki address (Käenkuja 4) [werstas.we-1613705, werstas.we-1613706, werstas.we-1613707].

Interpretation (separated from the above observations and based only on the cited metadata):

The 1921 record’s metadata indicates a political advertisement connected to a women’s organisation, which contrasts with mid-20th-century records whose metadata emphasizes commercial products, textiles and domestic goods (examples: the 1955 Askon ad, the 1956 OTK shirt ads, and the 1960 textile/wool ads) [werstas.we-1372484, lahdenmuseo.lkm-461598, werstas.we-1613705, werstas.we-1613706, werstas.we-1613707, hyvinkaa_mui.mui-25099].
The 1950 poster’s subjects (women’s rights movements; cooperative system; advertising) may indicate that gender and collective economic themes appear in advertising metadata at mid-century as well [ta_ah.ta-1369756].

Limitations and caution (must be read alongside the items above):

These statements are based only on catalogue metadata (titles, subjects, year fields) and do not confirm the actual visual or textual content of the items; the metadata should not be assumed to fully describe what appears in each image or poster [werstas.we-1372484, ta_ah.ta-1369756, hyvinkaa_mui.mui-25159, hyvinkaa_mui.mui-25099, lahdenmuseo.lkm-461598, werstas.we-1613705, werstas.we-1613706, werstas.we-1613707].

So a standard that speaks the national languages, but not Sámi, may push Sámi material out of view. That is a question about power, and the abstract promises to look at it.
What the test does. It runs every question twice, at the same time: search C with Finnish, Swedish and English names (as before), and search C with Northern Sámi names added. Nothing else changes, and the test checks that searches A and B came out the same both times.
The test ran on 30 October 2026 with 13 questions. Finto returned a Northern Sámi name for 42 of 44 thesaurus concepts used in search C, and the Sámi names added new search words in 12 questions.

section: 2. Would Annif describe the records the way cataloguers did?
text:
2. Would Annif describe the records the way cataloguers did?
Why this test. Annif is used to suggest subject words for new catalogue records. In the main study we only used it on the question. This test turns it around: Annif reads the title and description of each record the AI saw (never its subject words) and suggests subject words, which are then compared with the words the cataloguers chose. Words are compared through their YSO names in Finnish, Swedish and English, so naiset and women count as the same word.

Figure 1. How wide each search is
What it shows. For each question, how many records in the whole Finna index match search A (your own words), B (+ Annif) and C (+ thesaurus terms).
How to read it. One row per question, one dot per search. The scale is logarithmic: each step to the right is ten times more records. The grey line joins the smallest and the largest search. An open circle at “0” means the search matched nothing.
What it tells us. In the middle question, search C matches 4.4x as many records as A. Annif’s words (B) often change nothing: in 6 of 10 questions the green and blue dots sit on top of each other. The same chart, with the questions’ full names: What we found, section 1.

title: 9  Figures for the paper
section: Figure 2. How many records the searches share
text:
Figure 2. How many records the searches share



What it shows. How much of search A’s list of records searches B and C still contain, measured in two ways.
How to read it. 1 means the same records, 0 means none in common.

Left, Jaccard: records found by both searches, divided by records found by either. The order of the records does not matter.
Right, rank-biased overlap: the same idea, but agreement near the top of the lists counts most. The first ten records carry most of the weight, as they do for a researcher scrolling the results. Two searches can share many records (high Jaccard) but put different ones first (low rank-biased overlap).

“A kept no records” marks questions where the comparison is impossible.
What it tells us. On average B shares 62% of its records with A and C only 19%. At the top of the lists the agreement is 0.57 for B and 0.24 for C. The two measures can tell different stories: for Sawmill workers, A and C share many records (Jaccard 0.56) but put different ones first (rank-biased overlap 0.10).

title: 9  Figures for the paper
section: Figure 3. Which differences are bigger than chance
text:
Figure 3. Which differences are bigger than chance



What it shows. For five things (institutions, languages, material types, decades and subject words), how different the mix in search B or C is from search A, for each question.
How to read it. Each dot is one question. Further right means a more different mix: 0 is the same mix, 1 is nothing in common (the Jensen-Shannon divergence, the “difference score” of the other pages). Each dot has a grey tick: the difference that chance alone would give with this many records. It is found by drawing two samples of the same sizes from the two searches’ records put together, many times over. A filled dot is beyond its tick, a real difference. A hollow dot is within it, possibly just chance.
What it tells us. Between A and C the difference is bigger than chance for subject words in 8 of 10 questions, for institutions in 8 of 10, for languages in 4 of 10, for material types in 5 of 10 and for decades in 3 of 10. Between A and B the counts are much lower: subject words 3 of 10, institutions 3 of 10, languages 1 of 10, material types 2 of 10 and decades 1 of 10. The thesaurus terms change who and what is visible far more often than Annif’s words do.
